---
title: "Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)"
description: "A family of methods that adapts a pretrained model while training only a small subset of parameters or added components."
term: "Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)"
letter: "P"
category: "LLM Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a large pretrained model without
updating every weight. Instead, it trains a much smaller set of added or
selected values, reducing the memory and storage needed for adaptation.

## Technical explanation

PEFT methods freeze most pretrained parameters and optimize a compact
task-specific component. Examples include low-rank updates, adapter layers,
and learned prompt vectors. The choice determines where the trainable
parameters are inserted and how they interact with the frozen model.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

It can make adaptation more affordable when full fine-tuning does not fit
available compute or when many task-specific variants must be stored.
Trade-offs include task quality, training complexity, and compatibility with
the target inference stack.

## How it works

The base model's weights remain fixed while gradients update only the PEFT
parameters. At inference, the trained component is loaded alongside the base
model or merged into its weights if the method and deployment format support
merging.

## Practical example

An engineer can keep a pretrained language model frozen and train a low-rank
weight update for a domain-specific task. The result is a small adapter
artifact that can be used with the same base model rather than saving a full
copy of all its parameters.

## Common misconceptions

- PEFT still requires careful data preparation, evaluation, and deployment
  testing.
- Fewer trainable parameters do not guarantee lower inference latency;
  extra adapter operations can affect serving performance.
